summary: South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 31, prepared by the National Economic Board, covers April 1948, the month before the 10 May election. It reports voter registration of 7,730,000 (94 percent) and 939 candidates for 200 Assembly seats, communist violence including the Cheju-do revolt, and the Pyongyang North-South Conference attended by Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic. It records 15,848 refugees entering from the north, the first month of National Land Administration farm sales (28 percent sold), vested property disposal rules, and Military Government amnesty for 3,000 political prisoners. Economic chapters give prices, industrial output (paper, cotton, anthracite), coal and fertilizer imports, private trade (exports above imports), railroads, power, public works, budgets for F/Y 1948/49, bank deposits and note issue. Later chapters cover KILA, legal ordinances and the draft Civil Code, police, interzone mail and Radio Pyongyang, health, education, culture, press, youth and women. Useful for election-eve conditions and statistics.
highlights: A 10-day registration ending 9 April enrolled 7,730,000 voters, over 94 percent of those eligible, and 939 candidates, 17 of them women, contested 200 Assembly seats in the 10 May election.
The Pyongyang North-South Conference met 19-23 April with Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attending, and a 30 April joint communique rejected the southern election.
Cheju-do rioting began 3 April; communists attacked about 52 of 13,455 registration booths, and 29 rioters were killed in casualties reported for 3-19 April.
By 30 April, 28.7 percent of 587,974 former Japanese farms had been sold to farmers under Ordinance No. 173 through the National Land Administration.
15,848 refugees entered South Korea from the north in April, 20 percent above March, and a refugee ship sailed to Tientsin on 30 April for Mukden repatriates.
Railroads carried over 480,000 tons of freight, the most since October 1945, while March private imports reached 822.7 million won and exports of 654.1 million went over 93 percent to Hong Kong.
The Military Governor's amnesty freed over 3,000 minor political prisoners, and Judge Lobingier's proposed first Korean Civil Code was completed by the Department of Justice.
KILA met once on 19 April and adjourned 30 days by 23 to 0; bank deposits hit a record 55,305 million won and SKIG's overdraft a record 22,005 million.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of No. 31 (April 1948), SKIG and USAMGIK organization charts as of 1 January 1948, National Economic Board members under Chairman Dr. Wilhelm Anderson, and a six-part table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Arthur G. Peterson's overview: 94 percent of 7,730,000 voters registered despite communist terror, Cheju revolt and the Pyongyang conference. Over 15,000 refugees came south, 28 percent of Japanese-held farmland sold, and literacy reached 71 percent.

sections.title: Part I. Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Refugee arrivals and Korean schools in Japan, then vested property: Property Disposal sales rules, the simplified claims directive of 17 April, and rental data on 102,822 leases.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugee arrivals rose 20 percent over March to 15,848; the Kaesong camp was inspected. Osaka and Hyogo ordered Korean schools closed, leading to 73 parental arrests and about 4,000 protesters dispersed.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: Vested property covered sales rules for small businesses and homes, a simplified claims procedure, guaranteed bank loans for vested firms, audit decentralization and rental tables for 102,822 leases.

sections.title: Property Disposal
sections.summary: Rules for selling former Japanese small businesses and homes: auction or sealed bid, 20 percent down, 5 to 7 percent interest, 10-year contracts. Table 3 shows 96 April sales worth 62.4 million won.

sections.title: Claims Section
sections.summary: A 17 April directive simplified claims against vested property; only 50 of over 50,000 claims had been processed in a year. A seven-step OPC review now handles about 12 cases per day.

sections.title: Property Rentals
sections.summary: At 1 January 1948 there were 102,822 leases on 82,339 vested properties, with rents up in 83 percent of cases. Arrears were 87.2 million won; net rental revenue since 1945 was 283.5 million won.

sections.title: Part II. Production and Supply
sections.summary: Covers April 1948 agriculture (28.7 percent of former Japanese farms sold), prices, record paper and anthracite output, petroleum, trade with exports above imports, and labor disputes including the Seoul Electric streetcar case.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Fertilizer sales reached 35,091 metric tons. Under Ordinance No. 173, 28.7 percent of 587,974 former Japanese farms were sold by 30 April, priced at three times annual crop output.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Retail prices fell seasonally in April while wholesale prices barely moved. Seoul cleaned rice fell to 1,320 won per mal; National Price Administration controlled prices are given.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: March output rose over February: cotton yarn 28.5 percent, cotton cloth 26.2 percent. Paper hit a post-liberation record of 533.4 tons; government salterns produced 16,036 tons in April.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output hit a record 62,796 tons in March, 40,596 from Samchuk, but under half could be moved by rail. April bituminous imports from Japan were 83,171 tons.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: April 1948: the Consumer Goods Allocation Board set a 40/60 split between employees and the public; civilian supplies, petroleum (6,414,345 liters of gasoline) and 25,803 tons of salt were allocated. FFA distributed bonus goods worth 41,000,000 won.

sections.title: Petroleum
sections.summary: The Petroleum Distributing Company allocated 6.4 million liters of gasoline, 3.8 million of kerosene and 2.9 million of diesel in April. Sales were below March for most products; shortfalls were blamed on stock limits and late arrivals.

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: April permits (113 import, 94 export) implied exports of 443.8 million won against imports of 376.8 million. March exports of 654.1 million went over 93 percent to Hong Kong; government exports to Japan totaled $351,976.

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: General Dean's 7 April fact-finding committee recommended reorganizing Seoul Electric management and a union election. Marine Bureau talks continued, a Pusan stevedore petition was investigated, and the refugee-camp labor project was abandoned.

sections.title: Part III. Public Services
sections.summary: Covers transportation (railroads carrying over 480,000 tons), communications and Cheju sabotage, electricity deliveries of 75.9 million KWH, and public works including the Sumjingang dam.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: March Transportation revenue rose 119 percent to 283 million won, partly from a 161 million won Army payment. Railroads carried over 480,000 tons, the most since October 1945; Pusan received 48 percent of marine shipping space.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: Communist sabotage waned on the mainland but hit Cheju, where 16 poles were cut and 26 wires severed. The radio license fee rose from 40 to 50 won on 15 April.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: Electricity delivered in April totaled 75.9 million KWH. The Emergency Power Board met 7 and 21 April on conservation and a plan for a North Korean cutoff; the Pusan barge YFP-1 began production.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Road spending was virtually nil for lack of an appropriation, offset by volunteer labor. A Water Resources Committee met 2 and 23 April on the Sumjingang dam; 144 fires caused 76 million won in losses.

sections.title: Part IV. Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue fell to 28.2 billion won; SKIG overdraft hit a record 22,005 million. March bank deposits rose to a record 55,305 million won, while loans fell for the third month.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Note issue fell to 28.2 billion won, with 5,213 million returned since December. SKIG's overdraft hit a record 22,005 million; March revenue of 2,135 million was a record; 787 million in extra 1947/48 appropriations were authorized.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: March deposits rose 6,279 million won to a record 55,305 million, while loans fell 1,591 million. Ordinance No. 182 required exchange of Japanese-printed 100-won notes by 24 April; 39 loans totaling 713 million were approved.

sections.title: Part V. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Registration of 7,730,000 voters, KILA's April dissolution, the Pyongyang conference, 939 candidates, Ordinances 182-191, the draft Civil Code, police handling of Cheju-do violence, and interzone mail.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: Registration closed 9 April with 7,730,000 voters (over 94 percent) for 200 districts and 942 candidates. The Economic Board approved 400 million won irrigation credit and 250 million for Sumjingang Dam; Military Government personnel rose to 3,041.

sections.title: Section 2. Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA met only on 19 April, rejecting three resignations, tabling pending bills 20 to 0 and adjourning 30 days by 23 to 0. It had 90 members since December 1946 and passed 11 Public Acts.

sections.title: Section 3. Political Developments
sections.summary: The Pyongyang North-South Conference of 19-23 April, which Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attended, and election preparations: 939 candidates for 200 seats, rightist splits, and Choi Nung-chin's challenge to Rhee.

sections.title: North-South Conference
sections.summary: Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attended the Pyongyang sessions of 19-23 April; a resolution was signed by 16 parties and 45 organizations, and a 30 April communique rejected the southern election.

sections.title: Election Preparations
sections.summary: A rightist committee under O Sei-chang formed 1 April to speed the election. 939 candidates, including 17 women, sought 200 seats; Choi Nung-chin's challenge to Rhee was nullified on 7 May.

sections.title: Section 4. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Covers Ordinances 182-191, Hodge's Proclamation of Rights, Kaesong prison conditions, amnesty releases, and the draft Civil Code by Judge Lobingier with four books.

sections.title: Codification Bureau
sections.summary: The Department of Justice finished a proposed first Korean Civil Code, drafted by Judge Lobingier, who drew heavily on China's code. Its syllabus lists four books: Persons, Obligations, Property and Succession.

sections.title: Section 5. National Police
sections.summary: Police resented the court-warrant rule and the release of over 3,000 minor political prisoners. About 52 of 13,455 registration booths were attacked; Cheju-do rioting began 3 April, with 29 rioters killed by 19 April.

sections.title: Section 6. Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Mail exchange with North Korea became weekly from 15 April: 59,000 pieces against 37,000 in March. Radio Pyongyang attacked the southern election; Chough Pyong-ok reported 21 Koreans killed and 74 border violations.

sections.title: Part VI. Social
sections.summary: Covers cholera immunization and the Tientsin refugee ship, literacy at 71 percent, Arbor Day tree planting, the press on the 10 May election, Korean National Youth with 774,949 members, and women's election work.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Cholera immunization expanded along the coasts and 38th parallel. The refugee ship sailed to Tientsin on 30 April; 520,000 pounds of DDT arrived and 10,053 low-cost housing units were finished.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Literacy reportedly rose from 21 percent in 1945 to 71 percent by August 1947. The department was cut from 177 to 143 positions; 13,230,670 textbooks had been published since 1945.

sections.title: Section 3. Culture
sections.summary: Arbor Day, 5 April, became a national holiday with 100 million trees planted. Hodge presented instruments to the Korea Symphony Orchestra on 25 April; 58 athletes were selected for the London Olympics.

sections.title: Section 4. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press centred on the 10 May election and Pyongyang conference. It reported 91.7 percent registration and 939 candidates, 48 percent independents, plus Cheju-do disorders and anger at the closing of Korean schools in Japan.

sections.title: Section 5. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth mobilized 67,475 members on Arbor Day to plant 3,451,300 trees. Membership reached 774,949 by 30 April, with seven new training centers bringing the total to 62.

sections.title: Section 6. Women's Activities
sections.summary: The Women's Bureau gave over 50 election speeches, showed the film "The Peoples Choice" and published 5,000 copies of "New Homemaking." It also covered a mothers' school and a new home economics association.
